topic: National income and GDP: from a person's yearly income to a country's, what a product is (goods and services), GDP as the value of a year's final goods and services made inside the country, and six GDP rules taught one by one with small examples

book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook opens with the circular flow, defines national income, gives GDP's definition in one sentence ('market value of all final goods and services produced within the domestic territory in a year') and then explains each word. Here each word of that sentence is built separately from small things first: income over a year (two people), then 'product' (ketchup, flat, sofa, software, an insurer's plans), then 'value' (price tags), then 'domestic' (India's map), and only then the sentence; the remaining words become numbered rules, each with its own tiny case (spice packets for 'market', steel for 'final', an old laptop for 'produced this year'). The cost is that the most quoted phrase, final goods, appears in a caption before it is taught, one rule is taught in a doubtful form (unsold and self-used goods), and NDP, GNP, NNP are named but left for later.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Take the standard GDP definition apart word by word; teach each word as a separate numbered rule with one everyday case and a yes/no picture of whether it reaches GDP.

narration.density: About 22 terms (income, financial year, national income, GDP, NDP, GNP, NNP, product, goods, services, physical and software products, raw material, finished goods, monetary value, gross, domestic, geographical boundary, self consumption, final goods, intermediate goods, value addition, double counting, consolidation, CSO) in about 10 minutes, a little over 2 per minute, at about 195 words per minute. Each rule gets its own case, so the pace suits class 9-12; the opening minute (four measures and 'most stable') front-loads names that are not taught here.

talmel_summary: Objects and numbers mostly land on their words: each product pops in as it is named, the cyan rule rows write on with their sentences, and the laptop figures appear as they are said. The picture is strongest where a line to the GDP map is ticked or crossed (sold packets, final goods, resale) and where the steel's ₹5 is bracketed into the tool's ₹15. Four transcript gaps (16.5-28.3, 260-277, 291.7-304.9, 455.4-469.6 s) fall on exactly the numbers that matter (Shyam's answer, the 100-packet setup, the ₹400 total, the tool's ₹15), so there the picture is the only record; tiles 2 and 20 sit inside gaps. Some numbers are shown but never spoken (₹10 and ₹5 tags, 10 cars, 5 tools).

voice.notes: About 195 words per minute, friendly classroom tone; each rule is announced as 'chaliye ab dekhte hain GDP ka third/fourth concept', which pairs with the on-screen tracker. Numbers are small and read plainly (5 rupees, 10 rupees, 10,000, 15,000). Questions are put to the viewer and the answer follows at once, except the shopkeeper question, which is handed to the comments. Recognition loses about 56 s across four stretches, which may be music, fast speech or long held words.

game_ideas.player_does: Stands at India's border as the GDP counter. Cards arrive: a car made by a foreign firm's Indian plant, an Indian firm's factory abroad, steel sold to a car maker, the finished car, a haircut, an insurance policy, an old laptop resold, a new laptop from a shop, a farmer's own grain. The player drops each into the GDP basket or the 'not this year / not final / not here' bin.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each accepted card adds its value to the GDP bar and draws a ticked line to the map; rejected cards show their reason (outside the border, already inside another price, made in an earlier year).
game_ideas.win: The GDP bar ends at the correct total with no double counting.
game_ideas.lose: Accepting the steel and the car shows the steel's value counted twice and the bar overshoots; accepting the old laptop shows a past year's production being counted again.
game_ideas.concept: rule 4: final goods count, intermediate goods do not

game_ideas.player_does: Runs a value chain: a steel maker sells 1 kg steel, a tool maker adds labour, machinery, transport and profit, a shop sells the tool; the player sets each stage's price and decides what to enter in the GDP ledger.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each stage's price builds on the last (5, then 15, then a shop margin), and the ledger shows either the final price or the sum of value added at each stage; both reach the same total.
game_ideas.win: Ledger equals the final price (or the sum of value added) at every stage.
game_ideas.lose: Entering every stage's full price makes the ledger bar grow past the tool's price and an 'already included' bracket flashes over the repeated ₹5.
game_ideas.concept: why: double counting (steel inside the tool's price)

game_ideas.player_does: Places factories on a map, each with its owner's flag (Indian or foreign), some inside India's border and some abroad, then runs one year of production.
game_ideas.process_happens: Goods from factories inside the border flow into India's GDP bar, whoever owns them; goods from an Indian-owned factory abroad flow to the other country's bar.
game_ideas.win: Predict which bar each factory feeds.
game_ideas.lose: Putting an Indian firm's foreign plant into India's GDP shows its output arriving at the other country's map instead, which sets up GNP for the next lesson.
game_ideas.concept: rules 1-2: Indian or foreign company producing in India counts

checks_learned: Every rule stated as fact must be checked against national-accounts conventions before reuse: unsold stock (change in inventories) and own-account production of goods are part of GDP, unlike what rule 3 says here.

Institution facts need a date and a source: the CSO was merged into the National Statistical Office in 2019 under the statistics ministry; ministry names and office-holders said aloud must be verified or left out.
Numbers on screen and in the transcript must agree (Shyam 2 lakh vs 2,000); a mismatch is either a recognition error to recheck or a script error.
A term must not appear on screen before it is taught (final goods in a caption at 180 s, taught at 364 s).
Transcript gaps over 10 s that cover a number on screen (packets, ₹400, ₹15) must be flagged and the line re-recorded or re-transcribed.
A question handed to the viewer (shopkeeper's margin) must be answered somewhere in the course; BIE should schedule the answer in the next lesson's recall or in the notes.
Lessons with several rules should show a visible step tracker and a growing rule list, as here; a check can require one for any lesson with more than three numbered points.
Measures named in the opening (NDP, GNP, NNP) but not taught should be marked 'next lesson' on screen, not left as live branches.
Real brands (spice maker, steel maker, software firms, insurer's website, resale site) are replaced with generic ones.

teaching_best.why: A person's yearly income is the bridge to a country's national income; the same band simply swaps people for flags.
'Product' is built from objects at home, then a ketchup line from tomatoes, then an insurer's own 'products' page for services, so goods and services both feel like products before the definition.
The GDP definition is cut into numbered rules with a visible tracker and a growing rule list, so the learner always knows which rule of six is being taught.
Double counting is shown with tiny numbers (₹5 steel inside a ₹15 tool) and an 'already included' bracket, which makes the reason for 'final goods only' concrete.
An old laptop resale gives a clean 'no new production' case, and the shopkeeper variant is set as a thinking question (consolidation).

teaching_weak.why: Rule 3 is taught in a doubtful form: unsold godown stock and goods taken home are said to be outside GDP.
The office that computes GDP is named with an outdated office, a wrong ministry name and an office-holder; this dates the lesson and may be wrong.
'GDP is the most stable measure' is asserted and deferred, and NDP, GNP, NNP are only spelled out.
The shopkeeper question, which would teach that trade margins count, is left to the comments with no answer in the lesson.
About 56 s across four stretches are not recognised, and they hold the key numbers; the spoken lesson alone would be hard to follow there.
